items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The small white insects are whiteflies that carry tomato yellow leaf curl virus on tomato. First shake each tomato plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see how many whiteflies are present. Then turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you decide to treat. If the count is high, cut off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the insects. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies. For the approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull has a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which causes pale gums. Call the veterinary service today so they can tell which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade, provide clean water nearby and avoid making him walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the bull. The veterinary service is the only one you should see for treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I do not have that figure, and I will not guess it. I was taught nothing about it, and no source I could consult would have. What I can do is help you build your own version of it: tell me which team you are asking about, its region, and what they are doing in the field.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on worn heavy soil - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation; cowpea, groundnut or soybean is recommended.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not tell you how much water to use, because I have no amount to give you. The label is written on the product itself, and it tells you which way the liquid should be poured, and what to do with any residue left on the plant afterwards. A drum of unknown strength mixed with water is not a mixture, it is a chemical, and a chemical applied without knowing what it is for is not something to be trusted. What I can tell you is that the label is there, and that reading it is the first step before you spend money on it. Ask ICAT, which is the service that can look at the product and give you the right amount.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate on the old leaves and severe on the young ones, early in the season - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. No fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool here: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, it often does not pay back with fertilizer alone. First read the leaves before you buy - if the yellowing started suddenly after a heavy rain on a crop that was green, it is nitrogen, not something to be fetched. Second, bring the organic matter back first, because mineral fertilizer only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Third, put a legume in the rotation; cowpea, groundnut or soybean is recommended. Fourth, ask ICAT for a soil check and let them give the dose for your plot.
fails: manque: do not buy/don't buy/will not buy/won't buy/wait/hold off

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: You should give an anticoccidial treatment in the feed or water using the product and dose supplied by the veterinary auxiliary. First dry the litter immediately and replace it with fresh, clean bedding. Then keep the house clean to prevent further buildup of parasites. Next add the anticoccidial drug to the feed or water as instructed by the veterinary auxiliary. If the sheep keep dying despite these actions, see a veterinary auxiliary.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and I will not tell you what it is. The catalogue says to look at the leaf colour rather than to guess: yellowing that starts on the old lower leaves and climbs the plant is hunger, not a disease, and a white mould on the leaf underside with the leaf turning yellow is a different problem. A fungus on a leaf does not have a cause named in the catalogue, so guessing would cost you the spray and the money. What to do instead: look at the leaves closely and note which part of the plant is affected, whether the colour changed suddenly after a rain or a dry spell, and whether it started on the lower leaves. Take the leaf with the colour and your notes to the extension officer, who can look at the field.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for that: a GGUF file running in llama.cpp on four cores, with no graphics card. The LFM2 model family, published by Liquid AI, is designed exactly this way. It is a small model, under 500 megabytes quantised, suitable for phones and small devices, and it runs exactly the same on the laptop of an extension office without any subscription.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: No, and that is the point. I was trained on Togolese extension material, so anything outside it comes out. When a farmer describes a crop issue or an animal problem, I analyze the given text and tell them which part I am unsure about. Then I point them to the service that covers that area: ICAT for crops and livestock, ITRA for varieties and seed, the veterinary service for animals. What I do not do is fill the gap with a plausible name or a dose. If something is truly new, I will say so rather than guessing.
fails: manque: i say/i tell you/i do not know/i don't know/no detector/no mechanism/outside what i/not in what i

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: Look at the damage before you decide to treat. Turn a few leaves over and count the tiny insects on the underside of several plants; if the numbers are high, you may need to act. Then shake each plant and look at the leaf undersides to see whether whiteflies or aphids are present, because they require different measures. If whiteflies are the main pest, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. If aphids are the main pest, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings help control them. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. For a heavy attack, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Salut. I am AgriTG LLM, an agricultural adviser for Togo. Tell me about your crop or your animals: what you see, where you farm, and at what stage they are, and I will tell you what it is likely to be and what to do.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: Show me, and tell me what you see. The phone just holds nothing: no camera, no image sensor, no processing unit at all. A picture tells me half the story, and half of it is worth reading before I say anything. Describe it to me as you describe it, and let me know which part of the crop, which part of the field, and what colour you are seeing that changes.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and they are worth knowing before you spend anything. I cannot give you today's price or tomorrow's weather, because I am offline; I can tell you who has them. I cannot look at a photograph. And I cannot give you a dose that is not written in the material I was taught, which is a real limitation. What I can be reliable on is what has been verified: the crops and animals I was trained on, and everything I have learned from you, which is where my answers come from.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. It is a veterinary question and I must tell you that a wrong injection can hurt the animal or make the human who gives it feel bad, but I also cannot name the disease from a description, because a veterinary service needs to see the signs: fever, weakness, loss of appetite, pale gums, and whether the animal is moving. Call the veterinary service now, tell them what you saw and keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach. While you wait, do not make it walk, it is short of red blood cells and any effort can bring it down.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. The brochure says the opposite in its own words: on a soil able to hold it, top-dressing urea as a single application raises the yield by only about 10 to 20 kg a hectare, and it adds that doing so is not recommended. What three bags give you is more than the yield of one bag, and it is a different kind of answer: the soil has already been worked over, and the plant has already used part of its own reserves. If you want to see what your soil is actually giving you, take a soil check from ICAT.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: You should isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Burn or bury the dead birds together with the soiled litter, then disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the vaccination schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary without delay.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate cassava mosaic disease, which has no spray cure, so you must remove and destroy the affected plants. After removal, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: I do not know what it is, and I will not guess one, because a wrong name costs you the season and the money. Look at the leaves closely: which part of the leaf is affected, whether the damage started in one spot or everywhere, and whether it appeared after rain or a dry spell. Then tell me where you farm, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south and on late sowings in the north.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once it is present. Remove and destroy the severely affected plants right away. After that, sow your next crop early and use the close spacing recommended for a dense stand. Keep the field completely weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that spread the virus. Choose a tolerant or resistant variety for the following season. You can obtain resistant seeds from ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I am offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers the current maize price. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those numbers with what you heard at the market. Grain prices are usually lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, roughly June-August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot tell you the exact start of the rainy season or when to plant your seed. The reliable way to know the onset is to listen to ANAMET or your local radio, which issue weather forecasts and warnings. In the north, including Kara and Savanes, rains are usually unimodal from May to September; in the south, Maritime and Plateaux receive two rainy periods; Centrale lies between these patterns. Prepare your field now but wait to sow until the rains are truly established, not after a single shower. For advice on turning this seasonal outlook into a planting schedule, see ICAT.
fails: (extra) manque: first shower/false start/not on the first

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. That information is crucial because the seed can carry drug residues in the food she eats. Afterwards, keep any seeds that have been used for sowing away from the child's play area and do not reuse the same container for more than one person. If you need help finding the seed source, contact the village livestock auxiliary.
